Should a person ever be able to sue for an incident that happened while that person was committing a crime? If so, why?

I don't think there's an easy answer. The example I think most people would recognize would be harming yourself breaking into someone's home or something like that. I guess my rule of thumb would kinda be that if you wouldn't have had the incident occur if you hadn't committed the crime, you can't sue. So I can't be sued for shooting a home invader, but /u/Xanthia's drunk driver could have hit you even if you weren't robbing the pet store, for instance.

There are obvious details that need resolving, so I don't think it's really safe to say there's a general rule, and (as many things are) most incidents should be taken case-by-case.

The biggest problem with saying "no" is that I could bait you into committing a simple crime, then have carte blanche to fuck you over. So long as I can muddy the waters enough for reasonable doubt at my criminal trial, you / your estate suddenly has no recourse. Yes. In fact landowners can be liable for the actions of or injuries to trespassers. Generally a landowner is not liable if a person gets injured while trespassing provided the landowner did not know they were trespassing and was generally unaware of the danger posed to trespassers. If I own private property I use to hunt deer and I have knowledge that people regularly cut through my private drive on that land to get to a state park on the other side, I could be held liable if I accidentally shoot or injure them and I've never posted signs warning about the danger or informed the public of the use of my private land.

Under the theory of premises liability, landowners are generally required to maintain their property so when someone enters the property they have a reasonable belief that they will not be injured. That usually applies to people you invite on your property or are allowed to be there (mail man, lawn service, etc.). If a landowner knows -- or should know -- that there are frequent trespassers on their property, they will be liable for any injuries caused by an unsafe condition on the property if:

  1. the condition is one the owner created or maintained;
  2. the condition was likely to cause death or serious bodily harm;
  3. the condition was such that the owner had reason to believe trespassers would not discover it; and,
  4. the owner failed to exercise reasonable care to warn trespassers of the condition and the risk presented.

The law requires a bit more action on the landowner's part in maintaining the premises when children are trespassing on their property.
